title: Fiber Node Factory
problemStatement: Implement `createFiberNode(tag, type, props)` that initializes a Fiber node with `child: null`, `sibling: null`, `return: null`, `memoizedProps`, and `alternate: null`.
interviewTrap: Confusing `pendingProps` (props being passed to the new render) with `memoizedProps` (props from the last committed render).

detailedExplanation.conceptualOverview: React represents UI as a singly linked list of Fiber nodes (`child`, `sibling`, `return`). Render phase is interruptible and can be paused; commit phase is strictly synchronous.
stepByStepWalkthrough: 1. Initialize execution context and environment records for Fiber Node Structure & Pointers.
2. Execute logic adhering to ECMAScript standard specification.
3. Verify invariant boundaries and edge conditions.
detailedExplanation.underlyingEngineInternals: In JavaScript engines (e.g. V8), Fiber Node Structure & Pointers is optimized via inline caches, heap contexts, and bytecode translation.
edgeCasesHandled: Confusing `pendingProps` (props being passed to the new render) with `memoizedProps` (props from the last committed render).

verifiedRules: Adheres to ECMAScript runtime evaluation specifications.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: What is a Fiber Node in React and what are its core pointers?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: A Fiber Node is a plain JavaScript object representing a unit of work. It replaces recursive call stack frames with linked-list pointers: `child` (points to first child), `sibling` (points to next sibling), and `return` (points to parent fiber). This structure allows React to traverse, pause, resume, and abort rendering loops without call stack limitations.

interviewCrossQuestions.question: What is the purpose of the 'alternate' pointer on a Fiber node?
interviewCrossQuestions.answer: The `alternate` pointer links the currently rendered Fiber (`current`) to its counterpart being constructed in memory (`workInProgress`). React uses a Double Buffering strategy: it recycles the alternate fiber on re-renders, avoiding garbage collection object churn.
interviewCrossQuestions.whyAsked: Tests understanding of React's memory allocation and double-buffering strategy.

realWorldUseCases.description: The internal representation of all components in React applications.
realWorldUseCases.codeSnippet: function FiberNode(tag, pendingProps, key) { this.child = null; this.sibling = null; this.return = null; }

howToExplain.opening: A Fiber node is a unit of work with child, sibling, and return linked-list pointers that transforms component hierarchy into an interruptible work queue.
keyPoints: Replaced the synchronous recursive Stack Reconciler in React 16.
Linked-list pointers (child, sibling, return) enable iterative tree traversal.
Stores memoizedState, memoizedProps, and pending work flags.
Alternate pointer provides double buffering to minimize GC overhead.
howToExplain.closingImpression: Fiber transformed React from a synchronous UI library into an asynchronous UI operating system.
analogies: A git repository: 'current' is the main production branch; 'workInProgress' is a feature branch where you make changes, merging (committing) when complete.

commonMistakes.mistake: Confusing Fiber nodes with React Elements.
commonMistakes.why: React Elements are ephemeral objects created by JSX on every render. Fibers are persistent, stateful nodes that survive across renders.
commonMistakes.correct: Clarify that Elements are transient descriptors; Fibers are persistent units of work.

followUpDeepDive.question: How do React Lanes replace expiration times in Fiber priority scheduling?
followUpDeepDive.answer: In React 17+, Lanes use 31-bit integers where each bit represents a priority lane (SyncLane, InputContinuousLane, DefaultLane). Bitwise operators (`&`, `|`) allow React to combine, check, and defer priority groups in O(1) CPU operations.
